title: Concurrency — GCD & Swift Structured Concurrency
summary: Dispatch queues, async/await, actors, and Task as Swift's concrete concurrency model — how work moves off the main thread and back, and the two mistakes that cause frozen UI or silent data races.

slides.markdown:
Every iOS app has one non-negotiable rule: **UIKit and SwiftUI only render from the main thread.** Anything expensive — a network call, image decoding, a database query — has to run elsewhere, and the result has to hop back to main before it touches the UI.

Apple's answer to 'how do I run work elsewhere' has evolved twice: **Grand Central Dispatch (GCD)**, the queue-based model that shipped with iOS's earliest days, and **Swift's structured concurrency** (`async`/`await`, actors, `Task`), which replaced deeply nested completion handlers with code that reads top-to-bottom while still being genuinely asynchronous. Most production codebases today run both, and knowing when each is the right tool is the actual skill.

slides.sectionTitle: GCD vs structured concurrency for a new codebase
slides.markdown:
| | GCD | Structured concurrency |
|---|---|---|
| Readability for chained async work | nested closures | linear, top-to-bottom |
| Data race protection | manual (locks, serial queues) | compiler-enforced via actors |
| Cancellation | manual bookkeeping | built into Task, propagates automatically |
| Ecosystem maturity | universal, every API supports it | modern, minimum iOS 13 for async/await, 15+ for full actor ergonomics |

For new code targeting a reasonably current minimum iOS version, structured concurrency is the default: less error-prone, better cancellation, compiler-checked data-race safety. GCD still shows up for interop with older APIs that only offer completion handlers, and for a few low-level primitives (dispatch groups, barriers) that don't have a clean structured-concurrency equivalent yet.
